e-4415.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Nilpotent Matrix
e-4415.worked_solution:
Computing $B^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{2} & =B\cdot B \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 9 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since $B^2=O,$ the matrix $B$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$

e-4416.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
e-4416.worked_solution:
First, we compute $C^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{2} & 0 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $C^2=C,$ so $C$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute $C^5$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{5} & ={C}^{2}\cdot {C}^{2}\cdot C \\  & =C\cdot C\cdot C \\  & ={C}^{2}\cdot C \\  & =C\cdot C \\  & ={C}^{2} \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
Computing ${T}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{2} & =T\cdot T \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${T}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $T$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${T}^{6}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{6} & ={T}^{2}\cdot {T}^{4} \\  & =O\cdot {T}^{4} \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{T}^{6}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Nilpotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
Computing ${T}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{2} & =T\cdot T \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${T}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $T$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${T}^{6}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{6} & ={T}^{2}\cdot {T}^{4} \\  & =O\cdot {T}^{4} \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{T}^{6}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{3} & ={B}^{2}\cdot B \\  & =O\cdot B \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  

$$
{B}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Nilpotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
Computing ${B}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{2} & =B\cdot B \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${B}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $B$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${B}^{3}$ quickly, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{3} & ={B}^{2}\cdot B \\  & =O\cdot B \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  

$$
{B}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
Computing ${R}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{2} & =R\cdot R \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ -8 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${R}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $R$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${R}^{5}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}^{5} & ={R}^{2}\cdot {R}^{3} \\  & =O\cdot {R}^{3} \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{R}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: B² = [[25−25, 125−125], [−5+5, −25+25]] = O. Thus B⁶ = (B²)³ = O, so option d is correct.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
Computing ${B}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{2} & =B\cdot B \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 25 \\ -1 & -5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 & 25 \\ -1 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${B}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $B$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${B}^{6}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{B}^{6} & ={B}^{2}\cdot {B}^{4} \\  & =O\cdot {B}^{4} \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{B}^{6}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Computing K2, we have

K2=K⋅K=[927−3−9]⋅[927−3−9]=[0000]=O.

Notice that, since K2=O, the matrix K is a nilpotent matrix of index 2.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of a Nilpotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
Computing ${K}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{2} & =K\cdot K \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 27 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}9 & 27 \\ -3 & -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that, since ${K}^{2}=O,$ the matrix $K$ is a nilpotent matrix of index $2.$ 

We can use this fact to compute ${K}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{K}^{2} & ={K}^{2}\cdot {K}^{2} \\  & =O\cdot O \\  & =O\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
{K}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

decision.explanation: Multiplication gives A² = [[1,0,0],[0,4−2,4−2],[0,−2+1,−2+1]] = A. Thus A is idempotent, and A⁴ = (A²)² = A, matching option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${A}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${A}^{2}=A,$ so $A$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${A}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & ={A}^{2}\cdot {A}^{2} \\  & =A\cdot A \\  & ={A}^{2} \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{A}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we compute A2 as follows:

A2=A⋅A=[1000220−1−1]⋅[1000220−1−1]=[1000220−1−1]=A

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${A}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${A}^{2}=A,$ so $A$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${A}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{4} & ={A}^{2}\cdot {A}^{2} \\  & =A\cdot A \\  & ={A}^{2} \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{A}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${C}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${C}^{2}=C,$ so $C$ is an idempotent matrix.

We can use this fact to compute ${C}^{3}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{3} & ={C}^{2}\cdot C \\  & =C\cdot C \\  & ={C}^{2} \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{C}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

verification.explanation: Direct multiplication gives C² = [[0,0,2],[3,1,6−6−6],[0,0,1]] = C. Hence C³ = C²C = C, confirming option d and the revealed solution. The deliberately submitted option e is incorrect.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${C}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{2} & =C\cdot C \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${C}^{2}=C,$ so $C$ is an idempotent matrix.

We can use this fact to compute ${C}^{3}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{3} & ={C}^{2}\cdot C \\  & =C\cdot C \\  & ={C}^{2} \\  & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{C}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${E}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{2} & =E\cdot E \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${E}^{2}=E,$ so $E$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${E}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{4} & ={E}^{2}\cdot {E}^{2} \\  & =E\cdot E \\  & ={E}^{2} \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{E}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${E}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{2} & =E\cdot E \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${E}^{2}=E,$ so $E$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${E}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}^{4} & ={E}^{2}\cdot {E}^{2} \\  & =E\cdot E \\  & ={E}^{2} \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{E}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 9 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${D}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =D\cdot D \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${D}^{2}=D,$ so $D$ is an idempotent matrix.

We can use this fact to compute ${D}^{3}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}\cdot D \\  & =D\cdot D \\  & ={D}^{2} \\  & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{D}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${D}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =D\cdot D \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${D}^{2}=D,$ so $D$ is an idempotent matrix.

We can use this fact to compute ${D}^{3}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{3} & ={D}^{2}\cdot D \\  & =D\cdot D \\  & ={D}^{2} \\  & =D\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{D}^{3}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} & \frac{1}{4} \\ 1 & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

\begin{aligned}{W}^{2} & =W\cdot W \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =W\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${W}^{2}=W,$ so $W$ is an idempotent matrix. 

We can use this fact to compute ${W}^{4}$ quickly, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{4} & ={W}^{2}\cdot {W}^{2} \\  & =W\cdot W \\  & ={W}^{2} \\  & =W\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{W}^{4}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Power of an Idempotent Matrix
content.worked_solution:
First, we compute ${W}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}^{2} & =W\cdot W \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =W\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that ${W}^{2}=W,$ so $W$ is an idempotent matrix.
